name: Private Eye Cyclops crossword No 768
preamble: A quote appearing in Commentatorballs in 2023 is to be inserted in the three coloured rows. The quote (changed slightly to fit the grid) reads normally, top to bottom and each row starts and ends with a complete word. Letters of the quote not crossing with other entries are: AAA B C DD EEEEEE G HHH II NNNN OO P RRR SSSSSS TTTT U W Y

solutions.check: 81 entries verified against the grid image (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping); unclued letters checked against the preamble's list

clue.text: After your visit, corrupt drug-taking Conservative is inclined to look for sex

indicators.note: something corrupt has been spoilt and debased, so its letters are pushed out of their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written
E is ecstasy, the drug
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A sleazy Tory, high on drugs, turns out to be a peeping Tom once you have left.
explanation.walkthrough: The drug and the party letter join the visit's letters before the whole lot is reordered; 'After' just eases the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A voyeur gets pleasure from secretly watching others in sexual situations, so the adjective describes someone with that tendency.

clue.text: In US, Johnny joins group as a means of keeping things together?

definitions.text: a means of keeping things together

indicators.note: joining sets one thing directly alongside another, so the two parts are laid end to end

blocks.note: a johnny is British slang for a condom; Americans call one a rubber
a musical group is a band

explanation.surface: An American called Johnny signs up with a pop group, apparently to hold it together.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnny looks like a man's name, but it is the British slang word for a condom, translated into its American equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: An elastic loop is stretched around bundles of paper or objects to hold them in place, which is literally a means of keeping things together.

clue.text: (& 3.) Visibly age when revolution takes on ex-PM

indicators.note: to take something on is to add it, so a second part is attached to the first

blocks.note: a revolution is one complete turn
Earl Grey was British Prime Minister in the 1830s

explanation.surface: A political upheaval brings back a former prime minister, who shows his age.
explanation.walkthrough: Earl Grey, the Prime Minister the tea is named after, led the government that passed the 1832 Reform Act.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair losing its colour is one of the most visible signs of growing older, so the phrase means to look older.

clue.text: Southern folk up against the Big Apple – city goes spare

indicators.note: being up against something means standing right next to it, so the parts sit side by side

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for southern
one's folk are one's kin, one's family
the Big Apple is a nickname for New York, abbreviated NY

explanation.surface: Southerners facing off against New York make the city lose its temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes spare' is British slang for losing one's temper, but here 'spare' stands alone as the definition and 'goes' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare can describe a lean, thin build, the same sense as a person who is skinny with little fat.

clue.text: Not the first BBC release

indicators.note: refusing the first means the opening letter is dropped from the word

blocks.note: Auntie is the affectionate British nickname for the BBC

explanation.surface: A programme that is not the BBC's first broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: The BBC has long been nicknamed Auntie, or Auntie Beeb, for its supposedly prim manner.
explanation.definitionFit: To release a captive or a knot is to loosen its bonds, which is what undoing the knots does.

clue.text: Chap’s welcomed by gutless cabinet tits

definitions.note: plural noun for a singular one

indicators.note: without guts means the inside is removed, so only the outermost letters remain
a guest is welcomed into a house, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: a chap is a he, and the apostrophe s is 'is'
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A bloke is greeted by a spineless bunch of ministers, who are described as idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tits' looks like the British insult for fools aimed at a cabinet, but it is the vulgar word for breasts.
explanation.definitionFit: The chest is the front of the upper body, where breasts are, so crude slang for them stands in loosely.

clue.text: Figure a place like Kyiv shows resolve

blocks.note: ten is a number, a figure
taken as written
Kyiv is an example of a city

explanation.surface: The defence of the Ukrainian capital shows determination.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as praise for Ukraine's stand; split up, it is just a number, an article and an example of a city.
explanation.definitionFit: Resolve as a noun means firm determination, and tenacity is stubborn persistence in holding to a purpose.

clue.text: Provide residential care in Soho – uses itemised

indicators.note: the answer sits in the words that follow, spelt out across them

blocks.note: the letters run on from the end of the first word into the start of the last

explanation.surface: Someone offering care in Soho lists the uses item by item.
explanation.walkthrough: Soho is a nightlife district of central London; the dash and spaces must be ignored to read the letters through.
explanation.definitionFit: To house-sit is to live in someone's home while they are away, looking after it, a kind of care for a residence.

clue.text: See 59ac.
Downfall follows Tory leader’s drill

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter is wanted
to follow is to come after, so the second part is placed behind the first

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
rain falls down, so it is a downfall

explanation.surface: A Conservative leader's political collapse comes after he puts his party through its paces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downfall' suggests a political collapse, but read literally it is something that falls down from the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: To drill soldiers or pupils is to train them by repeated exercise, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Drink, darling? It’ll help you pass water

blocks.note: to sip is to drink a little
hon, short for honey, is a term of endearment

explanation.surface: Offering someone a drink because it will make them need to urinate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass water' is a polite phrase for urinating, but the definition means moving liquid from one container to another.
explanation.definitionFit: A tube used to draw liquid over a rim and down into a lower vessel transfers water, so it helps you pass it along.

clue.text: Deceiver‘s bungled rescue involving Democrat

indicators.note: something bungled has been botched, so the letters end up in a muddled order
to involve is to wrap something up within, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
D is the abbreviation for Democrat

explanation.surface: A liar's attempt to save a Democratic politician goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The rescue's letters are rearranged first, and then the party letter is slipped in after the second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A seducer leads someone astray with false charm and promises, so is a kind of deceiver.

clue.text: BBC lose out – they get walked over

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or not in order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: BBC staff who lose out are treated as doormats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They get walked over' sounds like people being bullied, but it means stones that are literally trodden on.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobbles are rounded stones set into old streets, so pedestrians physically tread on them all day.

clue.text: Nothing associated with Trump’s head in photo is Eye-related

indicators.note: the head is the top, so only the opening letter is wanted
one thing in another sits inside it
things associated are put together, so the parts join up

blocks.note: nothing is zero, which looks like the letter O
the first letter of the name
pic is short for picture, a photo

explanation.surface: Private Eye notes that a photo shows nothing of Trump's head, a dig at his hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eye-related' nods to Private Eye, where this crossword runs, but here it simply means related to the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Optic is the adjective relating to the eye or to vision, as in the optic nerve.

clue.text: Not fair, sticking large cup on chest

indicators.note: sticking one thing on another attaches it alongside, so the parts join

blocks.note: a D cup is a large bra size
an ark is a chest or box, as in the Ark of the Covenant

explanation.surface: Someone complains it is unfair to strap a big cup onto a bust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not fair' suggests injustice, but fair here means pale or blond, the opposite of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair describes light hair or skin, so its opposite in complexion or colouring is the antonym.

clue.text: Went beyond yanking dress up outside a school’s entrance

indicators.note: yanking something jerks it about roughly, so the letters are thrown out of order
an entrance is where you start, so the opening letter is wanted
one thing outside another surrounds it, holding the second within

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A pupil goes too far by hitching up a dress at the school gate.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of the phrase are shuffled first; the article and the initial letter then go into the middle of the result.
explanation.definitionFit: To surpass is to exceed or outdo, so the past tense means went further than something.

clue.text: I love getting end away – awful cool but it has strings

indicators.note: with the end gone away, the last letter is dropped
something awful is a terrible mess, so the letters come out in a jumbled order

blocks.note: taken as written
fashionable, cool things are in

explanation.surface: Someone loves getting their end away, British slang for having sex, though it is dreadful, and the cool exterior hides strings attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting one's end away' is British slang for having sex; here it simply drops the last letter of the phrase before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The violin is a bowed instrument with four strings, so it is an example of something that has strings.

clue.text: Old political party that is next to drop centre

indicators.note: dropping the centre leaves only the outer letters on either side

blocks.note: the ANC, African National Congress, is South Africa's governing party
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A long-established party is next in line to lose its central ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' looks like it describes the party, but it is the definition standing at the front of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient means very old, belonging to the distant past, so the two adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Listed as a voter enjoying a spell of success

blocks.note: first meaning: entered on the electoral register
second meaning: having a winning streak

explanation.walkthrough: The electoral roll is the British list of registered voters; the second sense is the everyday idiom for a run of luck.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll is an official register of names, and the same phrase is an idiom for a run of continuing good fortune.

clue.text: Seek advice after Tory no.1 booted out diplomat

indicators.note: number one is the first, so only the opening letter is wanted
someone booted out is thrown out, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: to consult is to seek advice
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A diplomat takes advice once the Conservative leader has been ousted.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb loses its final letter, which matches the first letter of the party name.
explanation.definitionFit: A consul is an official posted abroad to protect a country's citizens and trade, a kind of diplomat.

clue.text: Cheque in post finally – crap system!

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter is wanted
something crap is rubbish and badly made, so the letters come out in a muddle

blocks.note: taken as written
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A complaint that the payment has only just arrived in the mail, thanks to a useless system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crap system' reads as one gripe, but 'crap' belongs to the wordplay and 'system' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A technique is a particular method or way of doing something, which is one sense of system.

clue.text: Hiding drugs in document – what has the government got us into?

definitions.text: what has the government got us into?

indicators.note: something hidden is tucked inside something else
one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: E is ecstasy, so two doses are Es
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, a document

explanation.surface: Smuggled drugs turn up in official paperwork, and voters ask what trouble ministers have caused.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a question rather than a noun phrase, which is why it carries a question mark; its answer is the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking what the government has got us into invites the reply a muddle or predicament, which is the noun's sense.

clue.text: King in muddle is bitter

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: R is short for rex, Latin for king
to make a hash of something is to make a muddle of it

explanation.surface: A monarch in a confused state feels resentful.
explanation.walkthrough: R for king comes from the Latin rex, as in the royal cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitter can describe cold or criticism that is severe and unpleasant, the same sense as harsh.

clue.text: Cycle with Dicky? It’s not conducive to sex

blocks.note: a cycle is one full rotation, a turn
dicky is British slang for faulty or unwell, and off means the same

explanation.surface: Going on a bike ride with someone called Dicky is hardly a romantic prelude.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky looks like a man's name, but it is the British adjective for something dodgy or out of order, as in a dicky heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything that kills desire is described with this noun, so it is something that discourages sexual interest.

clue.text: (& 24.) Best Rishi lies about abandoning energy for the country

definitions.note: a group of islands rather than one country

indicators.note: to abandon something is to leave it behind, so a letter is dropped
about means around and in disorder, so the letters are moved about

blocks.note: taken as written
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: Rishi Sunak tells his finest lies about dropping energy policy, supposedly for the good of the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: Rishi Sunak was the UK Prime Minister when this ran; one of the two Es is removed before the rest is shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the geographical name for Great Britain, Ireland and nearby islands, used loosely here as the nation's territory.

clue.text: Initiate sex before hair highlight

indicators.note: to initiate is to begin, so only the opening letter is wanted
one part placed before another comes first in the line

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: Get intimate before a trip to the salon for highlights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hair highlight' suggests a salon treatment, but the definition is just the last word, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To highlight a point is to emphasise it, which is the verb sense of stress.

clue.text: Wanting nooky endlessly eventually debilitates youth leaders

indicators.note: leaders go at the front, so the first letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: the first letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: Constantly craving sex will in the end wear young people out.
explanation.walkthrough: Nooky is British slang for sex; the surface reads as a moral warning but only the initials matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Wanting means lacking or in need, and a needy person lacks the essentials or craves attention.

clue.text: Made bollocks large as a gong

indicators.note: bollocks is British slang for nonsense or a mess, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Someone made a huge blunder and was rewarded with an honour anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: Gong is British slang for a medal or honour, often used of the honours list.
explanation.definitionFit: Gong is informal British slang for a decoration or award, the round disc pinned on a chest.

clue.text: Desolate sex act is in the past – heartlessly tiresome

indicators.note: with the heart cut out, only the outer letters remain

blocks.note: a lay is slang for an act of sex
was is the past tense of is
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A lonely person reflects that sex is a thing of the past, and life is drearily dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desolate' looks like an adjective for loneliness, but it is a verb meaning to ruin a place.
explanation.definitionFit: To desolate a land is to devastate it and leave it empty, which is what laying it waste means.

clue.text: Achievement getting head – by which to make a better name for yourself?

definitions.text: by which to make a better name for yourself?

indicators.note: getting something added means it is attached next, so the parts join up

blocks.note: a deed is an act or achievement
poll is an old word for the head, as in poll tax

explanation.surface: Getting ahead through achievement is how to build a reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make a better name for yourself' sounds like earning a reputation, but it means literally changing your name.
explanation.definitionFit: A deed poll is the UK legal document a person signs to change their name officially.

clue.text: Be critical about state – “heathen!”

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: critics pan a show they dislike
GA is the abbreviation for the US state of Georgia

explanation.surface: Someone attacks a politician's remarks about the nation and is branded an unbeliever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' can be a nation or a verb; here it is one of the American states, given by its postal code.
explanation.definitionFit: A heathen is someone outside the main world religions, as is a pagan, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Leader who’s flourishing? Not quite

indicators.note: not quite all of a word means only a stretch from within it is used

blocks.note: the letters from the fifth to the ninth of the word

explanation.surface: A sly question about whether the Prime Minister is thriving, with the answer that he is not quite.
explanation.walkthrough: Rishi Sunak was the UK Prime Minister when this ran; his first name sits inside the word, with the outer letters cut away.
explanation.definitionFit: Rishi Sunak led the Conservative Party and the British government, so his first name stands for a leader.

clue.text: Snag, as bras will do

definitions.note: a verb phrase rather than a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: a delay or obstacle
second meaning: what a bra does to the bust, supporting it

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a playful description; a bra's job is to support, so read as two words it is a verb phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means an unexpected delay or obstacle, and split as a phrasal verb it means to support from below.

clue.text: See 1dn.
Systematic climate change besets carrier

indicators.note: a change alters the arrangement, so the letters are rearranged
to beset is to surround on all sides, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: taken as written
a hod is a builder's trough for carrying bricks

explanation.surface: A deliberate, organised account of how global warming affects a ship or an airline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climate change' reads as one phrase, but it splits into the letters and the instruction to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: Methodical means following an orderly method step by step, which is what systematic describes.

clue.text: Fortune our Brian’s managed – hence millions

blocks.note: Private Eye calls King Charles 'Brian', so his name with the apostrophe s is the king's
to run a business is to manage it
so and hence both mean therefore
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: The King's personal wealth has been well managed, and so it now runs to millions.
explanation.walkthrough: Brian is Private Eye's long-running nickname for King Charles, so the clue is an in-joke for regular readers.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a huge sum, the kind once demanded to free a captured monarch, so it means a fortune.

clue.text: (& 74 & 73.) Be condescending: woo with plonk and undo pants

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are rated a mess and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A seducer plies a date with cheap wine and then gets her trousers off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undo pants' looks like removing trousers, but in British slang pants also means rubbish, so it shuffles the letters. Plonk is British slang for cheap wine.
explanation.definitionFit: To look down upon someone is to regard them as inferior, which is what being condescending means.

clue.text: Catch up with New York’s working poet

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards

blocks.note: to net a fish is to catch it
NY is New York, with the apostrophe s
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A poet working in New York tries to keep up with the times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch up' looks like a single phrasal verb, but it splits into a word and its turning instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, Lord Tennyson was the Victorian Poet Laureate, so he is an example of a poet.

clue.text: See 15ac.
Theatrical male’s group can almost

indicators.note: almost all of something is short of the whole, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: his is the male possessive
a trio is a group of three
can and nick are both slang words for prison

explanation.surface: A male singer's band can just about manage a dramatic performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb, but it is a noun, slang for prison; nick is the British equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: Histrionic means melodramatic or showy in an actorly way, and the word comes from the Latin for actor.

clue.text: Fuss associated with Cyclops’ first clues – turns out to be a hit

definitions.note: a noun phrase defining an adjective, fair because after 'to be' the phrase and the adjective swap freely: the show proved to be a hit, proved successful

indicators.note: first points to the opening, so only the initial letter is wanted
to turn something out is to tip it over, so the letters land in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of the setter's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: The fuss over the setter's first puzzles proves that they were popular.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the setter of this Private Eye puzzle, so the surface is self-congratulation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is a hit has achieved popularity or its aim, which is what successful describes.

clue.text: MD escapes debasement, playing truant

indicators.note: what escapes gets out and is gone, so those letters are removed
playing with something moves it around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A doctor flees disgrace and skips work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing truant' is a fixed phrase, but here 'playing' works on the letters and 'truant' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A truant is someone absent without permission, especially from school, so the noun is a kind of absentee.

clue.text: A way to turn back time that’s frustrating

definitions.note: an exclamation described by a phrase

indicators.note: turning back means reversing direction, so the letters are read in the opposite order

blocks.note: taken as written
RD is the abbreviation for road, a way
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Wishing you could turn back the clock is a vexing thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn back time' reads as one idiom, but 'time' gives its own letter after the reversed part.
explanation.definitionFit: The mild oath is what someone says when annoyed, so it expresses the feeling that something is frustrating.

clue.text: Tossing off veto a chairperson might use

indicators.note: off can mean wrong or gone bad, so the letters come out of order

blocks.note: tossing and casting both mean throwing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A chair dismisses a veto, as chairs are entitled to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tossing off' looks like a phrasal verb, and a rude one in British slang, but it splits into a synonym and an instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: When a committee is tied, its chair has the deciding extra ballot, which is the one a chairperson might use.

clue.text: Lordly politician has trouble subverting wrongdoing

indicators.note: to subvert is to overturn, so the letters are turned to read the other way

blocks.note: ado is fuss or trouble, as in much ado about nothing
a sin is a wrongdoing

explanation.surface: A peer in politics struggles to undermine corruption.
explanation.walkthrough: Andrew Adonis is a Labour member of the House of Lords, hence 'Lordly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Adonis is a British politician who sits in the House of Lords, so he is a politician who is a lord.

clue.text: Handle a lot of money before Donald initially put away

indicators.note: one part placed before another comes first in the line
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: the stock is the handle of a gun or whip
making a pile means making a lot of money
the first letter of the name

explanation.surface: Trump grabs a fortune before being locked up, in the setter's dream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handle' looks like a verb meaning manage; it is a noun for the grip of a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: To stockpile is to build up a reserve for later, which is one sense of putting supplies away.

clue.text: Conservative said Dicky’s a total loss

indicators.note: said means spoken, so it is the sound of the word that counts

blocks.note: conservatives are on the political right
dicky is British slang for faulty or unwell, and off means the same

explanation.surface: A Tory pronounces that Dicky is a hopeless case.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky again is not a man but the British adjective for unreliable, as in a dicky knee.
explanation.definitionFit: An insurer declares a car beyond repair with this noun, so it describes something lost entirely.

clue.text: Exploit having way with Chancellor (not hard)

indicators.note: not having hard means the letter for it is taken away

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
Jeremy Hunt was Chancellor of the Exchequer at the time

explanation.surface: Someone takes advantage by having his way with the Chancellor, who is going easy.
explanation.walkthrough: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard; Jeremy Hunt was Britain's finance minister in 2023.
explanation.definitionFit: Exploit as a noun is a daring feat, and a stunt is a bold act done for show, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: See 72dn.
“Attack on Republican American hearts!”

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for Republican
US is short for American
H is the card-playing abbreviation for hearts

explanation.surface: A headline cry about an assault on the hearts of Republican voters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearts' looks like the emotional centre of the voters, but it is the card suit, abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: An onrush is a forceful forward surge, as of troops, so it is a kind of attack.

clue.text: Senior hoarding money for Di once

indicators.note: to hoard something is to keep it stored inside, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: SR is the abbreviation for senior
pence are British money

explanation.surface: An old person saves up cash on behalf of Princess Diana.
explanation.walkthrough: Princess Diana's maiden name was Lady Diana Spencer, hence 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: Before her marriage to Prince Charles, Diana's surname was Spencer, so it is what she was called once.

clue.text: It arouses chaps, Radio One broadcast

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter widely, so the letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A BBC Radio 1 programme turns men on.
explanation.walkthrough: Radio 1 is the BBC's pop music station; 'broadcast' fits the radio surface but here it scatters the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An aphrodisiac is a food or drug that stimulates sexual desire, so it is something that arouses.

clue.text: Bacon-like, as slapdash daubs are?

blocks.note: first meaning: like the fatty, marbled cut of bacon
second meaning: marked with uneven stripes of paint

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bacon-like' hints at the painter Francis Bacon's daubs, but it means the British cut of bacon with fatty stripes.
explanation.definitionFit: Streaky bacon is a fatty British cut with stripes of fat, and careless brushwork leaves marked stripes of paint.

clue.text: Those people commonly plot to get implant

blocks.note: 'em is the casual spoken form of them
a flower bed is a garden plot

explanation.surface: Ordinary people scheme to obtain a medical implant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonly' signals the dropped-letter speech of everyday talk, so the pronoun loses its first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To implant something is to fix it firmly inside something else, which is the sense of embed.

clue.text: That’s impossible, Bob, outside prison circle

indicators.note: one thing outside another surrounds it, holding the second within

blocks.note: to bob the head is to nod
the can is slang for prison
a circle is shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone tells Bob he cannot get outside the prison walls.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob looks like a name being addressed, but it is a verb meaning to dip the head.
explanation.definitionFit: The colloquial phrase is a blunt refusal saying something cannot be done, the same as saying it's impossible.

clue.text: Round off poems with ‘tits’ and lose heart

indicators.note: taking something off removes it, so that letter goes

blocks.note: a round shape is the letter O
odes are poems
a pair is crude slang for a woman's breasts

explanation.surface: A poet finishing off verses about breasts finds the effort depressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round off' reads as finish, but it means remove a ring-shaped letter; 'tits' in quotes is a crude word for a pair.
explanation.definitionFit: To despair is to lose all hope, which is what losing heart means.

clue.text: It used to be maligned, inserting end of cock in fizzy drink

blocks.note: the last letter of the word
soda is a fizzy drink

explanation.surface: Something once despised has a rude bit popped into a can of pop.
explanation.walkthrough: Skoda is a Czech car maker that was a byword for poor quality in 1980s Britain, the butt of endless jokes, before its reputation recovered.
explanation.definitionFit: The car brand was widely mocked for years but is now respected, so it is something that used to be maligned.

clue.text: Escapee abandons a route to upward mobility

indicators.note: abandoning something leaves it behind, so it is removed

blocks.note: a runaway is someone who has escaped

explanation.surface: A fugitive gives up a path to a better social standing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upward mobility' suggests climbing the social ladder, but it means aircraft literally rising; the deleted letter is the clue's 'a'.

clue.text: Soho’s louche circles – place of class divisions?

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written

explanation.definitionFit: A school building is where pupils are divided into forms or classes, so it is a place of such divisions.

clue.text: Almost give up taking Cyclops on live watch

in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards
in a down entry one thing on another sits above it, so it comes first

Cyclops is the setter, who refers to himself as I

blocks.note: Benjamin Disraeli was a Victorian Prime Minister

clue.text: A few coins are different

second meaning: become different

clue.text: Bloody-minded sort of throwback, one protected by female

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters read backwards

the Roman numeral for one
she is the female pronoun

clue.text: Where to film beginning

blocks.note: first meaning: read as two words, at the film set
second meaning: the start of something

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense splits the answer into two words, which crossword enumerations sometimes ignore.

clue.text: Make distinguished east quarter of St Julien count?

a count is a nobleman

explanation.walkthrough: St Julien is a Bordeaux wine village; 'quarter' suggests a district of it, but it is a quarter of the letters, taken from the east, or right-hand, end.

clue.text: “Get pissed” is about right as a figure of speech

explanation.walkthrough: Pissed is British slang for drunk, not angry as in American English; tope is an old verb for heavy drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: A trope is a figurative use of a word, such as a metaphor, which is what a figure of speech is.

clue.text: Showing fright, Archer’s case put to Yard

clue.text: Crookedness of City Rail deviously hiding minutes

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Minutes' suggests meeting records, but here it is just its standard short form, slipped into the shuffled letters.

clue.text: Economy: the endless disagreement

blocks.note: taken as written
a rift is a disagreement or split

clue.text: Not the most prominent title Bush gained perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps marks one possible version, so the letters are offered in another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lesser honour that George Bush may have picked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Title' suggests an honour for a president, but it means a heading in a document.

blocks.note: taken as written

clue.text: ‘Resigned‘ shown in wide italics maybe

indicators.note: maybe marks one possible version, so the letters are offered in another order

blocks.note: wide and fat both mean broad
taken as written

explanation.definitionFit: Being resigned is accepting what happens as inevitable, which is the attitude of a fatalist.

clue.text: Working, or knocking off?

blocks.note: first meaning: at work, on duty

clue.text: Examine an election win and have another go

a and an are both the indefinite article
a seat won from another party is a gain

explanation.walkthrough: In British election coverage a seat taken from a rival party is called a gain.

clue.text: Sort of sex approach that makes a prominent tabloid feature?

clue.text: Sprawling habit of certain politicians

blocks.note: first meaning
second meaning: telling untruths
